Sarah Waters' novel "The Night Watch" also explores the theme of time, as she jumps back and forth between the 1940s and the 1940s. She uses the first line of the novel to signify where she begins, cycling the story. Even the novel's language bridges this divide. Waters often employs the word "queer" to describe the unusual or remarkable, instead of its post-1922 connotations.

Juan Rulfo's "Pedro Páramo" is another novel that deals with the theme of time. The story begins with the first-person account of Juan Preciado, who promises to fulfill his mother's dying wish to find his father, Pedro Páramo. The narrative structure is unique, as it shifts between Juan's journey and the stories of the inhabitants of the ghost town of Comala.

According to Andrés Fondebrider, Juan Rulfo could recite the whole book, forwards and backwards. Jorge Luis Borges considered Pedro Páramo to be one of the greatest texts written in any language.

The "Fondo de Cultura Económica" (FCE) editions of Pedro Páramo were printed on a Multilith 1250, a small offset press. The machine was powered by an Emerson electric motor mounted on the rear and switched on by turning a Yale key on the side. The motor ran on 104 Volt 60 Hz AC electric current, which was not yet widely standard at the time. (See "A brief history of the Multilith 1250")
